about.title: Choking First Aid: What First-Aid Courses Teach
about.length_note: This class runs a little over the 8-minute aim. It covers three age groups (adult, child, infant), the 911 call, and a caregiver note on swallowing difficulty. You can stop after any beat and pick up again later.

Choking first aid advice for an adult

say.text: Welcome to class 7. Today we look at what first-aid courses teach about choking. Think of it as a summary to help you plan, not as medical advice.

show.text: Choking First Aid: What First-Aid Courses Teach

say.text: This class does not replace a hands-on first-aid or CPR class. It does not replace the person's own doctors either. We will finish by planning how to book a class.

show.text: Not a substitute for a class

say.text: First, what is choking? The airway is blocked, partly or fully. Food or a small toy can do it. So can swelling, or fluids such as vomit.

show.text: Choking = a blocked airway

say.text: Why does this matter? The Red Cross says a person who is choking can quickly become unresponsive. So it helps to know the signs early.

show.text: Act quickly

say.text: Now the big question: coughing, or choking? Courses teach that a person who can cough forcefully should keep coughing. Stay close and watch.

show.text: Coughing hard: can cough, speak or cry. Let them keep coughing, and stay with them. || Choking: cannot speak, cry or cough forcefully. They need help now.

ask.q: Sam is coughing loudly and can say, "I'm fine." What do courses teach?
ask.right: Let Sam keep coughing, stay close, and watch for any change.
wrong: Leave the room until it stops
ask.why: Forceful coughing might clear the object by itself. The choking steps are for someone who cannot cough, talk, cry or laugh forcefully.

say.text: So what does choking look like? Hands clutched at the throat, and a panicked look. The person cannot talk. Breathing may be noisy, or the cough weak. The skin turns pale or bluish.

show.text: Hands at the throat • Panicked or confused look • Cannot talk • Noisy or squeaky breathing • Weak cough • Pale or bluish skin

say.text: Caregiver note. Some people cannot clutch their throat or call out. Courses teach you to watch the face, the breathing and the skin colour. Ask your instructor how that looks for the person you care for.

show.text: A caregiver sitting beside a person at a table, watching their face and breathing during a meal

say.text: Now, calling 911. If two people are there, courses teach that one calls 911 while the other gives first aid. The AHA steps list calling 911 first.

show.text: Call 911

say.text: If you can, put the phone on speaker next to the person. Stay on the line. 911 call-takers are trained to give instructions for choking. Follow what they tell you.

show.text: Phone on speaker, next to the person • Stay on the line • Follow the call-taker

ask.q: Why stay on the line with 911 during a choking emergency?
ask.right: The call-taker can tell you what to do, step by step, until help arrives.
wrong: Call-takers only record your name and then leave
You must hang up so that help can find you
The phone has to be free for the person to call you back
ask.why: Choking is one of the emergencies where call-takers give instructions to the caller. They tell you what to do until help arrives.

say.text: Call-takers' scripts and local services differ from place to place. Check with your local 911 center about how they help callers. Class 5 shows you how to make a 911 card for the phone.

show.text: Check with your local 911 center

say.text: Now the steps courses teach for an adult who cannot cough, speak or breathe. Step one: stand to the side and slightly behind. Give five back blows between the shoulder blades.

show.text: 5 back blows

say.text: Step two: five abdominal thrusts. Courses teach you to make a fist just above the navel and cover it with your other hand. Then you give quick inward and upward thrusts.

show.text: A fist placed just above the navel with the other hand over it, pulling inward and upward

say.text: Then you alternate: five back blows, then five abdominal thrusts. Keep going until the object comes out or the person becomes unresponsive. The Red Cross and the AHA teach this pattern.

show.text: 5 back blows • 5 abdominal thrusts • Repeat until the object is out or the person is unresponsive

ask.q: For an adult who cannot cough, speak or breathe, what order do these courses teach?
ask.right: Five back blows, then five abdominal thrusts, and keep alternating.
wrong: Five abdominal thrusts only, and never back blows
Ten back blows in a row, then stop
Chest thrusts first, then a drink of water
ask.why: The Red Cross and the AHA both teach alternating five back blows with five abdominal thrusts for adults.

say.text: Children get the same steps, with gentler force. For a small child you may need to kneel behind them. Courses also say never to hang a child upside down.

show.text: Children: same steps, gentle but firm

say.text: What if the person uses a wheelchair? A Red Cross resource for healthcare providers says you may need to kneel. A hands-on class is where you practise adapting.

show.text: A caregiver kneeling behind a person seated in a wheelchair

say.text: Babies are different. Courses teach face-down along your forearm, head lower than the body, with five firm back blows. Then turn the baby face-up for five chest thrusts. Never abdominal thrusts.

show.text: Adult and child: 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts || Infant: 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts

ask.q: Which of these is NOT taught for a choking baby?
wrong: Keeping the head lower than the body
ask.why: The AHA and the Red Cross both say abdominal thrusts are not used on infants. Babies get back blows and chest thrusts.

say.text: What if the person becomes unresponsive? Courses teach you to lower them to a firm, flat surface. Then you start CPR, beginning with compressions. The call-taker will guide you.

show.text: Unresponsive: start CPR

say.text: Afterwards, even if the object came out, experts say a child or infant who has had choking first aid should be checked by a doctor soon.

show.text: Get checked by a doctor

say.text: Caregiver note. The Red Cross says some neurological or muscular conditions raise the risk of choking. Swallowing difficulty does too. Ask their doctors for their own plan, including for a feeding tube.

show.text: People with dysphagia have a higher risk of choking.

ask.q: You care for someone who has trouble swallowing or uses a feeding tube. What is the best step?
ask.right: Ask their doctors, or their swallowing specialist, for a plan made for that person. Still call 911 in an emergency.
wrong: Rely only on this class and skip the doctors
Copy a plan made for another person
Wait until a choking emergency happens to ask
ask.why: Their own doctors know their body and their needs. This class gives general course content, not a personal plan.

say.text: A swallowing specialist can work out a plan that fits the person. Add what you learn to the one-page medical sheet from class 4.

show.text: Their doctors, their plan

say.text: Now the most important step: take a hands-on class. The Red Cross and the AHA both offer first aid and CPR classes. You can find them online, in person, or blended.

show.text: American Red Cross: First Aid/CPR/AED • American Heart Association: Heartsaver First Aid CPR AED • Online, in person or blended

say.text: Why hands-on? The Red Cross says its online-only classes do not let you show your skills to an instructor. The AHA says CPR classes need a hands-on skills session for a card.

show.text: Practise with an instructor

say.text: Here is your plan. Look up a class near you. Ask the person's doctors about swallowing. Check with your local 911 center or fire department about local services.

show.text: 1. Find a Red Cross or AHA class • 2. Ask their doctors about swallowing • 3. Check with your local 911 center

ask.q: Which is the best next step after this class?
ask.right: Book a hands-on class, and ask the person's doctors about their swallowing plan.
wrong: Decide you are now fully trained
Practise abdominal thrusts on a friend for fun
Wait for an emergency to look for a class
ask.why: This class is a summary of what courses teach. Hands-on practice with an instructor is what builds the skill.

other_side.claim: For adults and children, current teaching is to alternate five back blows with five abdominal thrusts.
other_side.other_view: Teaching has changed over time. When the AHA announced its 2025 update, it noted that earlier guidelines gave no choking guidance for adults and recommended only abdominal thrusts for children. Some people may have learned an older method, which is one more reason to take a current class.

other_side.claim: If you are alone with a choking person, start first aid first and call after.
other_side.other_view: Mayo Clinic, citing the Red Cross, says a lone rescuer gives back blows and abdominal thrusts first. The AHA's choking steps begin with calling 911 immediately. Sources order the call differently, so ask your instructor and follow your 911 call-taker.

other_side.claim: Courses agree on every detail of what to do when the choking person becomes unresponsive.
other_side.other_view: The Red Cross steps for an unresponsive person include opening the person's mouth. The AHA article says not to use your fingers to search the mouth for an object. An instructor can show exactly what the course you take teaches.
